'''''Sporobolus heterolepis''''', commonly known as '''prairie dropseed''',<ref name="PLANTS">{{PLANTS |id=SPHE |taxon=Sporobolus heterolepis |accessdate=27 November 2015}}</ref> is a species of [[prairie]] grass native to the tallgrass and mixed grass prairies of central [[North America]] from [[Texas]] to southern [[Canada]].<ref name="PLANTS" /><ref>{{BONAP|ref |genus=Sporobolus |species=heterolepis}}</ref> It is also found further east,  to the Atlantic coast of the [[United States]] and [[Canada]], but is much less common beyond the [[Great Plains]] and is restricted to specialized habitats. It is found in 27 states and four Canadian provinces.<ref name="PLANTS" />

==Description==
Prairie dropseed is a perennial [[bunchgrass]] whose mound of leaves is typically from {{cvt|1|to|2|ft|cm|-1|abbr=on}} high and {{cvt|2|to|3|ft|cm|-1|abbr=on}} across. Its flowering stems ([[culm (botany)|culms]]) grow from {{cvt|1+1/2|to|3|ft|cm|round=5|abbr=on}} tall, extending above the leaves.<ref name="Illinois">{{Illinois Wildflowers|grasses/plants/pr_dropseed|Prairie Dropseed (''Sporobolus heterolepis'')}}</ref>

The flower cluster is an airy [[panicle]] {{cvt|3|to|8|in|cm|0|abbr=on}} long with many branches. They terminate in small [[spikelet]]s, which each contain a single fertile [[floret]]. When it blooms, the floret has three reddish [[anther]]s and a short feathery [[stigma (botany)|stigma]].<ref name="Illinois" /> If it is pollinated, the floret produces a nearly round seed {{cvt|1.5|to|2.0|mm|in|2|abbr=on}} long.<ref name="Minnesota">{{Minnesota Wildflowers|''Sporobolus heterolepis'' (prairie dropseed)|grass-sedge-rush|prairie-dropseed}}</ref>

At the base of the spikelet are two [[bract]]s ([[glume]]s), one of them {{cvt|4|to|6|mm|in|abbr=on}} long and the other {{cvt|2|to|4|mm|in|2}} long.<ref name="Illinois" /> The bracts each are long and tapered, with sharply pointed tips.<ref name="Minnesota" /> Around the floret are a [[lemma (botany)|lemma]] and [[palea (botany)|palea]], each about {{cvt|3.5|to|5.5|mm|in|abbr=on}} long,<ref name="Illinois" /> though the palea is sometimes longer than the lemma.<ref name="Minnesota" />

Prairie dropseed is a fine-textured grass with long, narrow leaves that arch outward, forming attractive, round tufts. The leaves range in color from a rich green hue in summer to a golden rust color in the fall. Foliage is resilient enough to resist flattening by snow, so it provides year-round interest. From late July to mid-September, the grass blooms with rusty-tan flowers that rise {{cvt|30|to|36|in|abbr=on}} in height.{{Citation needed|date=May 2026}}

==Ecology==

Prairie dropseed is a plant which typically only thrives in established prairie ecosystems, and does not easily establish when planted from seeds early in prairie restoration attempts.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fedewa |first=Chad A. |last2=Stewart |first2=J. Ryan |date=2009 |title=Seed Germination Characteristics of Prairie Dropseed (''Sporobolus heterolepis'') |url=https://doi.org/10.3375/043.029.0211 |journal=Natural Areas Journal |volume=29 |issue=2 |pages=188-192 |doi=10.3375/043.029.0211|url-access=subscription }} </ref> Once established, it is fairly hardy, being able to tolerate brief periods of drought, water inundation, and [[juglone]] toxicity from close proximity to [[Juglans nigra|black walnut]] trees.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mahr |first=Susan |date=2025 |title=Prairie dropseed, ''Sporobolus heterolepis'' |url=https://hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/prairie-dropseed-sporobolus-heterolepis/ |website=Wisconsin Horticulture, Division of Extension}}</ref> This plant is known to be an important part of the diet of several [[Lepidoptera|lepidopteran]] species.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Narem |first=Diane M. |last2=Meyer |first2=Mary H. |date=2017 |title=Native Prairie Graminoid Host Plants of Minnesota and Associated Lepidoptera: A Literature Review |url=https://doi.org/10.18473/lepi.71i4.a5 |journal=The Journal of the Lepidopterists' Society |volume=71 |issue=4 |pages=225-235 |doi=10.18473/lepi.71i4.a5|url-access=subscription }}</ref> While prairie dropseed often fails to establish in natural prairie ecosystems due to its slow growth, studies investigating its growth under controlled conditions have found that it favors warmer temperatures and moist soil for germination.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hockenberry Meyer |first=Mary |last2=Narem |first2=Diane M. |date=2019 |title=Prairie Dropseed Germination Highest with Warm, Moist Conditions |url=https://journals.ashs.org/view/journals/horttech/29/6/article-p830.xml |journal=Hort Technology |volume=29 |issue=6 |pages=830 - 832 |doi=10.21273/HORTTECH04407-19|doi-access=free }} </ref><ref>Brewer, Katherine. “Using Plugs and Hydrogels to Establish Populations of Prairie Dropseed, a Critical Native Grass, in Restored Prairies in Minnesota.” Ashs.org, 28 June 2022, journals.ashs.org/view/journals/hortsci/57/8/article-p851.xml Accessed 4 Mar. 2026.</ref>
